claim: In many mouse models of skin cancer, only a few tumors typically form even though many cells competent for tumorigenesis receive the same oncogenic stimuli.
source: In many mouse models of skin cancer, only a few tumors typically form even though many cells competent for tumorigenesis receive the same oncogenic stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about mouse models of skin cancer, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: microRNA-203 is downregulated by HrasG12V in keratinocytes.
source: We discover that microRNA-203 is downregulated by HrasG12V.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Loss of microRNA-203 promotes selection and expansion of tumor-initiating cells.
source: Using a knockout mouse model, we demonstrate that loss of microRNA-203 promotes selection and expansion of tumor-initiating cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from knockout mouse models shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: Restoration of microRNA-203 using an inducible model potently inhibits proliferation of tumor-initiating cells.
source: Conversely, restoration of microRNA-203 using an inducible model potently inhibits proliferation of these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from the inducible model shown in Figure 5.

claim: Over 1100 transcripts were differently expressed (two-fold change and FDR <0.05) in keratinocytes expressing HrasG12V, compared to the control.
source: Over 1100 transcripts were differently expressed (two-fold change and FDR <0.05) in keratinocytes expressing HrasG12V, compared to the control (Figure 1C and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results section and supported by 3Seq data.

claim: HrasG12V activates cellular migration pathways in keratinocytes.
source: Gene ontology functional analysis revealed profound deregulation in three core processes by HrasG12V: activation of cellular migration, upregulation of pro-angiogenic pathways, and suppression of the terminal differentiation program (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by gene ontology analysis of 3Seq data.

claim: HrasG12V upregulates pro-angiogenic pathways in keratinocytes.
source: Gene ontology functional analysis revealed profound deregulation in three core processes by HrasG12V: activation of cellular migration, upregulation of pro-angiogenic pathways, and suppression of the terminal differentiation program (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by gene ontology analysis of 3Seq data.

claim: HrasG12V suppresses the terminal differentiation program in keratinocytes.
source: Gene ontology functional analysis revealed profound deregulation in three core processes by HrasG12V: activation of cellular migration, upregulation of pro-angiogenic pathways, and suppression of the terminal differentiation program (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by gene ontology analysis of 3Seq data.

claim: Transcripts upregulated by HrasG12V in primary keratinocytes strongly and significantly overlapped with putative cancer stem cell signatures obtained from murine squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) models.
source: Importantly, transcripts upregulated by HrasG12V in our primary keratinocytes strongly and significantly overlapped with the putative cancer stem cell signatures obtained from murine squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) models (Schober and Fuchs, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by comparison with published data.

claim: Transcripts upregulated by HrasG12V significantly overlapped with transcripts known to be targets of the c-Fos transcription factor in a genetic model of SCC.
source: In addition, transcripts upregulated by HrasG12V significantly overlapped with transcripts known to be targets of the c-Fos transcription factor in a genetic model of SCC (Durchdewald et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by comparison with published data.

claim: 15 differentially expressed miRNAs were detected upon HrasG12V expression (FDR <0.05, two-fold change).
source: Overall, we detected 15 differentially expressed miRNAs upon HrasG12V expression (FDR <0.05, two-fold change) (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by miRNA-Seq data.

claim: miR-203 and miR-205 are strongly suppressed by HrasG12V.
source: First, the epithelial tissue-specific miRNAs, miR-203 and miR-205, which represent the most abundant miRNAs expressed in murine skin and primary keratinocytes were strongly suppressed by HrasG12V.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by miRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Members of the abundantly expressed, miR-23/24/27 miRNA cluster were downregulated by HrasG12V.
source: Additionally, members of the abundantly expressed, miR-23/24/27 miRNA cluster were also downregulated by HrasG12V.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by miRNA-Seq data.

claim: miR-21 was strongly induced by HrasG12V, becoming the most highly expressed miRNA.
source: Secondly, miR-21 was strongly induced becoming the most highly expressed miRNA, consistent with its direct activation by oncogenic Ras reported in other systems (Talotta et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by miRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: miR-146 was induced by HrasG12V but is expressed 2-orders of magnitude lower than miR-21.
source: miR-146 was also induced by HrasG12V. However, this miRNA is expressed 2-orders of magnitude lower than miR-21, suggesting that its upregulation may have limited contribution to Hras-initiated tumorigenesis at this early stage.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by miRNA-Seq data.

claim: The differential expression of miR-21, miR-203, and miR-205 measured by qPCR was nearly identical to the quantification by miR-Seq.
source: In support of the quantitative performance of our miR-Seq, the differential expression of all three miRNAs measured by qPCR was nearly identical to the quantification by our miR-Seq (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The repression of miR-203 by HrasG12V is most likely mediated by suppressing the production of primary miR-203 transcripts.
source: Collectively, we conclude that the repression of miR-203 by HrasG12V is most likely mediated by suppressing the production of primary miR-203 transcripts at an early stage of oncogenic cellular transformation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by 3Seq and qPCR data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: miR-203 expression was absent from epithelial compartments adjacent to tumor stroma in DMBA/TPA-induced papillomas.
source: Consistent with our in vitro results, miR-203 expression was absent from epithelial compartments adjacent to tumor stroma, the region where putative cancer stem cells reside.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: miR-203 expression levels were strongly reduced in tumor tissues compared to adjacent epidermal regions in DMBA/TPA-induced papillomas.
source: Overall, miR-203 expression levels were strongly reduced in tumor tissues compared to adjacent epidermal regions.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: miR-203 expression was gradually lost in a KrasG12D/Smad4cKO model where skin tumors progressed to invasive SCC through serial passages.
source: In an independent mouse model of SCC, we also found that miR-203 expression was gradually lost in a KrasG12D/Smad4cKO model where skin tumors progressed to invasive SCC through serial passages of tumors (White et al., 2013) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In human skin SCC samples, miR-203 was downregulated at the onset of tumorigenesis and progressively lost during the course of tumor progression.
source: In these human skin SCC samples, miR-203 was already downregulated at the onset of tumorigenesis and progressively lost during the course of tumor progression, similar to the pattern observed in the mouse models.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2G-O.

claim: In poorly differentiated human SCC samples, the miR-203 signal was completely absent, yet readily detectable in surrounding hyperplastic or normal epidermal regions.
source: In the poorly differentiated SCC samples, the miR-203 signal was completely absent, yet readily detectable in surrounding hyperplastic or normal epidermal regions (Figure 2G–O).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2G-O.

claim: A significant reduction in miR-203 and an elevation of miR-21 were detected in head and neck SCC samples compared to patient-matched normal tissues in TCGA data.
source: In addition, we mined publically available data sets from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and detected a significant reduction in miR-203 and an elevation of miR-21 in head and neck SCC samples compared to patient-matched normal tissues (Figure 2P).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 2P.

claim: miR-203 is located in an intergenic region, 3.3 kbp downstream from the Asp gene and 15.3 kbp upstream of the Kif26a gene.
source: We have characterized the genomic locus of miR-203 and determined that miR-203 is located in an intergenic region, 3.3 kbp downstream from the Asp gene and 15.3 kbp upstream of the Kif26a gene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: miR-203 null mice were born at the expected Mendelian ratio.
source: Both strains were born at the expected Mendelian ratio.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the miR-203 knockout mouse phenotype.

claim: miR-203 null mice showed no signs of gross developmental defects as adults.
source: They also showed no signs of gross developmental defects as adults (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by images shown in Figure 3D.

claim: miR-203 is highly expressed primarily in stratified epithelial tissues, such as the epidermis, tongue, esophagus, and cervix.
source: miR-203 is highly expressed primarily in stratified epithelial tissues, such as the epidermis, tongue, esophagus, and cervix, yet poorly expressed or absent in other tissues such as the small intestine, bladder, lung, kidney, liver, or brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: miR-203 begins to be expressed by E13 when the epidermis begins to stratify.
source: Because miR-203 begins to be expressed by E13 when the epidermis begins to stratify, we examined the proliferation rate and thickness of embryonic skin from E16 to P4.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as background information.

claim: At E16, miR-203 knockout mice showed a mild increase in cell proliferation as measured by BrdU incorporation.
source: At E16, we observed a mild increase in cell proliferation in the KO, as measured by BrdU incorporation (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The thickness of the miR-203 knockout epidermis was significantly increased at E16, compared to WT littermates (p = 0.03).
source: Although the difference in BrdU incorporation did not achieve statistical significance (p = 0.07), the thickness of the KO epidermis was significantly increased, compared to WT littermates (p = 0.03).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by epidermal thickness measurements.

claim: The increase in epidermal thickness in miR-203 knockout mice was most prominent at early stages (E16 and E17) and waned as skin development progressed (P4).
source: Interestingly, the increase in epidermal thickness was most prominent at early stages (E16 and E17) and waned as skin development progressed (P4) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by epidermal thickness measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: At P4, miR-203 knockout mice displayed normal histological development of the epidermis and hair follicles.
source: At P4, miR-203−/− mice displayed normal histological development of the epidermis and hair follicles, and the difference in proliferation and epidermal thickness between KO and WT became indistinguishable (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: No evidence of perturbed differentiation was found in miR-203 knockout mice based upon analysis of early and late epidermal differentiation markers, Keratin 1 and Loricrin.
source: In addition, we found no evidence of perturbed differentiation in miR-203−/− mice based upon analysis of early and late epidermal differentiation markers, Keratin 1 and Loricrin, for the spinous and granular layers, respectively (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3H,I.

claim: miR-203 limits cell division when the proliferation rate is high during early embryonic skin development but not at later stages when the proliferation rate wanes.
source: Together, these results provide evidence that miR-203 limits cell division when the proliferation rate is high during early embryonic skin development but not at later stages when the proliferation rate wanes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the embryonic skin development data.

claim: miR-203 knockout primary keratinocytes showed approximately two-fold higher colony-forming capacity compared to WT controls.
source: We observed ∼two-fold higher colony-forming capacity of miR-203−/− keratinocytes, compared to the WT controls (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Ad-Cre-treated miR-203fl/fl cells showed approximately two-fold higher colony-forming capacity compared to Ad-GFP-treated control cells.
source: We again observed a similar, ∼two-fold higher colony-forming capacity by the Ad-Cre-treated miR-203fl/fl cells compared to the Ad-GFP-treated control cells (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: miR-203 limits the clonogenicity of normal keratinocytes.
source: These results suggest that miR-203 limits the clonogenicity of normal keratinocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the colony formation assay data.

claim: miR-203 null animals developed approximately 2.5-fold more tumors compared to WT control animals in DMBA/TPA carcinogenesis.
source: Furthermore, miR-203 null animals developed ∼2.5-fold more tumors, when compared to WT control animals (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by tumor multiplicity data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Measurement of tumor sizes at week 17 showed no statistically significant difference in tumor sizes between miR-203 null and WT genotypes.
source: Measurement of tumor sizes at week 17 showed no statistically significant difference in tumor sizes between genotypes although miR-203 null animals were more susceptible to tumor formation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by tumor size distribution data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Loss of miR-203 increases the number of tumor-initiating cells but does not significantly alter the type of tumors.
source: These results suggest that loss of miR-203 increases the number of tumor-initiating cells but does not significantly alter the type of tumors for example, conferring tumors with more aggressive phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the DMBA/TPA carcinogenesis data.

claim: miR-203 WT and KO papillomas possess the canonical HrasQ61L mutation at similar frequencies, 80% and 85.7% respectively.
source: To further probe the mechanistic differences between miR-203 WT and KO tumors, we assessed the mutation spectra of these tumors and found that they possess the canonical HrasQ61L mutation at similar frequencies, 80% and 85.7% for WT and KO tumors, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The loss of miR-203 led to approximately 40% increase in colony-forming capacity immediately after the initial plating of HrasG12V transduced cells at passage 1.
source: At the passage 1, the loss of miR-203 led to ∼40% increase in colony-forming capacity immediately after the initial plating (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: miR-203 null cells generated more and bigger clones compared to WT control cells at each passage when transduced with HrasG12V.
source: Strikingly, in contrast to the WT cells that generally formed smaller colonies in subsequent passages, the miR-203 null cells generated more and bigger clones compared to WT control cells at each passage (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by serial passage assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Introduction of miR-203 resulted in suppression of keratinocyte proliferation and colony formation ability.
source: Introduction of miR-203 resulted in suppression of keratinocyte proliferation and colony formation ability (Figure 5C,D), as noted previously (Yi et al., 2008; Jackson et al., 2013; Benaich et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by colony formation and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Short-term (approximately 24 hr) induction of miR-203 completely abolished the gain of S-phase entry caused by oncogenic Hras.
source: Furthermore, whereas oncogenic Hras-enhanced S-phase entry, short-term (∼24 hr) induction of miR-203 completely abolished the gain of S-phase entry (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Continuous induction of miR-203 severely compromised the colony-forming capacity of HrasG12V transduced cells.
source: Over a longer term, continuous induction of miR-203 severely compromised the colony-forming capacity of the transduced cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No evidence for enhanced apoptosis caused by miR-203 was detected, as measured by the absence of sub-G1 keratinocytes.
source: We did not detect any evidence for enhanced apoptosis caused by miR-203, as measured by the absence of sub-G1 keratinocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on flow cytometry analysis.

claim: 294 transcripts were identified as candidates for miR-203 targets by demanding all potential targets be upregulated in all the miR-203 KO samples and downregulated in all the miR-203-induced samples.
source: By demanding all potential targets be upregulated in all the miR-203 KO samples and downregulated in all the miR-203-induced samples, we identified 294 transcripts as our candidates for miR-203 targets (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by meta-analysis of multiple expression datasets.

claim: Among the top 20 most differentially expressed transcripts when miR-203 was deleted or induced, 15 of them contain at least one 7-mer or 8-mer match in their 3′UTRs.
source: Among the top 20 most differentially expressed transcripts when miR-203 was deleted or induced, 15 of them contain at least one 7-mer or 8-mer match in their 3′UTRs (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by sequence analysis of candidate targets.

claim: An unbiased de novo motif search using the 3′UTRs of 294 candidate transcripts revealed that the most enriched motif (ACAUUUCA, p = 1 × 10−13) perfectly matched to nucleotide position 2–9 of miR-203, the 8-mer seed sequences of miR-203.
source: In support of this approach, an unbiased de novo motif search using the 3′UTRs of these 294 transcripts revealed that the most enriched motif (ACAUUUCA, p = 1 × 10−13) perfectly matched to nucleotide position 2–9 of miR-203, the 8-mer seed sequences of miR-203 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by de novo motif analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A total of 113 mRNAs were detected to have miR-203 seed containing Ago2 binding sites by HITS-CLIP.
source: A total of 113 mRNAs were detected to have miR-203 seed containing Ago2 binding sites.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Ago2 HITS-CLIP data.

claim: The motif corresponding to miR-203 detected by the HITS-CLIP was ACAUUUCA (p = 1 × 10−19), identical to the motif detected by transcriptome analysis.
source: The motif corresponding to miR-203 detected by the HITS-CLIP was also ACAUUUCA (p = 1 × 10−19), identical to the motif detected by our transcriptome analysis (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by de novo motif analysis of HITS-CLIP data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: No evidence for global regulation at the translation level for miR-203 targets was detected based on analysis of translational efficiency changes upon miR-203 deletion.
source: Finally, we did not detect any evidence for global regulation at the translation level for miR-203 targets based on our analysis of translational efficiency changes upon miR-203 deletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Key regulators in the Ras signaling pathway and important genes involved in regulation of cell division including Hbegf, Ccnd1, Snai2, Met, and Pola1 were identified as high-confidence targets of miR-203.
source: Importantly, we found a number of key regulators in the Ras signaling pathway and important genes involved in regulation of cell division including Hbegf, Ccnd1, Snai2, Met, and Pola1 in this list (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the combined analysis of expression data and HITS-CLIP shown in Figure 6F.

claim: miR-203 targets identified in the meta-analysis were enriched in the upregulated transcripts in HrasG12V-transformed keratinocytes, compared to non-targeted transcripts.
source: Overall, miR-203 targets identified in the meta-analysis were enriched in the upregulated transcripts in HrasG12V-transformed keratinocytes, compared to non-targeted transcripts, consistent with the downregulation of miR-203 in these cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by cumulative distribution analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pola1 is the catalytic subunit of the DNA-POL-alpha holoenzyme, which is required in initiation of DNA replication during S-phase.
source: Pola1 is the catalytic subunit of the DNA-POL-alpha holoenzyme, which is required in initiation of DNA replication during S-phase (Lehman and Kaguni, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as background information about Pola1.

claim: Hbegf is an Egf-like ligand that activates MAPK signaling through activation of EGF-receptors, Erbb1 and Erbb4.
source: Hbegf is an Egf-like ligand that activates MAPK signaling through activation of EGF-receptors, Erbb1 and Erbb4.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as background information about Hbegf.

claim: In keratinocytes, Hbegf is mitogenic and promotes keratinocyte migration.
source: In keratinocytes, Hbegf is mitogenic and promotes keratinocyte migration (Stoll et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as background information about Hbegf.

claim: In an epithelial cancer cell line, Hbegf acts as an oncogene promoting cell proliferation.
source: In an epithelial cancer cell line, Hbegf acts as an oncogene promoting cell proliferation (Miyamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as background information about Hbegf.

claim: Pola1 and Hbegf contain 3′ UTR miR-203 target sites (9-mer and 8-mer respectively) that are targeted by miR-203, validated by luciferase assay.
source: Pola1 and Hbegf contain 3′ UTR miR-203 target sites (9-mer and 8-mer respectively) that are targeted by miR-203, validated by luciferase assay (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In miR-203 null epidermis, both Pola1 and Hbegf mRNAs were elevated.
source: Furthermore, in miR-203 null epidermis, both Pola1 and Hbegf mRNAs were elevated (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Pola1 protein levels were elevated in the absence of miR-203, further elevated in the presence of HrasG12V, and repressed by miR-203 induction.
source: In addition to mRNA levels, Pola1 protein levels were also elevated in the absence of miR-203. It was further elevated in the presence of HrasG12V and repressed by miR-203 induction (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: The expression of Ccnd1 showed a strong negative correlation to miR-203.
source: Additionally, we observed that the expression of Ccnd1, an essential cell cycle regulator that is often induced or amplified by oncogenic Ras (Downward, 2003; Stransky et al., 2011), showed a strong negative correlation to miR-203 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Suppression of Hbegf and Pola1 strongly suppressed the growth potential of keratinocytes.
source: Suppression of Hbegf and Pola1 strongly suppressed the growth potential of keratinocytes (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by shRNA knockdown colony formation assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Knockdown of Hbegf and Pola1 in established miR-203+/+ and miR-203−/− keratinocytes transduced with HrasG12V resulted in potent suppression of keratinocyte growth potential.
source: Additionally, we knocked down Hbegf and Pola1 in established miR-203+/+ and miR-203−/− keratinocytes transduced with HrasG12V and similarly observed potent suppression of keratinocyte growth potential, demonstrating that these targets are also required in HrasG12V-transformed keratinocytes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: A considerable amount of 'molecular time' exists between the common ancestors that harbor the great majority of driver mutations and the phenotypically identified cancer cells that compose the bulk of the tumor in breast cancer.
source: When genome sequencing data were utilized to construct the history of cancer cells in breast cancer, it was revealed that a considerable amount of 'molecular time' exists between the common ancestors that harbor the great majority of driver mutations and the phenotypically identified cancer cells that compose the bulk of the tumor (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information from published literature.

claim: Lineage tracing experiments conducted in genetically engineered mouse models revealed that only a few clones give rise to tumors whereas a vast majority of mutated cells are unable to sustain tumorigenesis.
source: In support of these observations, lineage tracing experiments conducted in genetically engineered mouse models revealed that only a few clones give rise to tumors whereas a vast majority of mutated cells are unable to sustain tumorigenesis (Driessens et al., 2012; Schepers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information from published literature.

claim: Oncogenic Ras mutations are some of the most frequently detected driver mutations in human cancer.
source: Oncogenic Ras mutations are some of the most frequently detected driver mutations in human cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: Among the three Ras genes (H-, K-, and N-ras), Hras is commonly mutated in tumors originated from stratified epithelial tissues including squamous cell carcinoma in the skin, head, and neck cancer as well as bladder cancer.
source: Among the three Ras genes (H-, K-, and N-ras), Hras is commonly mutated in tumors originated from stratified epithelial tissues including squamous cell carcinoma in the skin, head, and neck cancer as well as bladder cancer (Bos, 1989; Agrawal et al., 2011; Stransky et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information from published literature.

claim: The vast majority of Ras mutations are missense, point mutations at amino acid residues glycine 12 (G12), glycine 13 (G13), or glutamine 61 (Q61).
source: Experimental and genomic sequencing studies have revealed that the vast majority of Ras mutations are missense, point mutations at amino acid residues glycine 12 (G12), glycine 13 (G13), or glutamine 61 (Q61) (Bos, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information from published literature.

claim: All Ras mutations at G12, G13, or Q61 generally interfere with the GTP binding pocket and compromise the GTPase activity of Ras proteins.
source: Structural and biochemical studies have further confirmed that all of these mutations generally interfere with the GTP binding pocket and compromise the GTPase activity of Ras proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: Ras mutations lead to uncontrolled activation of downstream effectors including Raf/MEK/ERK and PI(3)K pathways, resulting in sustained cell survival and proliferation observed in human cancers.
source: In turn, these mutations lead to uncontrolled activation of downstream effectors including Raf/MEK/ERK and PI(3)K pathways, resulting in sustained cell survival and proliferation observed in human cancers.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: Hras, Kras, and Nras all harbor multiple binding sites for the let-7 miRNA in their 3′UTRs.
source: Indeed, Hras, Kras, and Nras all harbor multiple binding sites for the let-7 miRNA, a founding member of miRNAs, in their 3′UTRs (Johnson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information from published literature.

claim: Impaired miRNA biogenesis in the form of Dicer1 disruption has been shown to be a tumor-suppressing mechanism for the development of Kras-induced lung cancer in a mouse model.
source: Additionally, impaired miRNA biogenesis in the form of Dicer1 disruption has been shown to be a tumor-suppressing mechanism for the development of Kras-induced lung cancer in a mouse model (Kumar et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information from published literature.

claim: miR-21, -29, and miR-17∼92 function as tumor-promoting miRNAs in Ras-induced tumorigenesis.
source: A number of individual miRNAs were also found to function as modifiers for Ras-induced tumorigenesis that include miR-21, -29, and miR-17∼92 as tumor-promoting miRNAs and miR-34, -15/16, and miR-143/145 as tumor-suppressing miRNAs (Kasinski and Slack, 2010; Iorio and Croce, 2012; Mendell and Olson, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information from published literature.

claim: miR-34, -15/16, and miR-143/145 function as tumor-suppressing miRNAs in Ras-induced tumorigenesis.
source: A number of individual miRNAs were also found to function as modifiers for Ras-induced tumorigenesis that include miR-21, -29, and miR-17∼92 as tumor-promoting miRNAs and miR-34, -15/16, and miR-143/145 as tumor-suppressing miRNAs (Kasinski and Slack, 2010; Iorio and Croce, 2012; Mendell and Olson, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information from published literature.

claim: miR-203 is the most highly expressed miRNA in the skin.
source: We discovered that miR-203, the most highly expressed miRNA in the skin (Yi et al., 2008; Jackson et al., 2013), is downregulated by HrasG12V.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous publications.

claim: Restoration of miR-203 suppresses human SCC metastasis.
source: Of note, a recent study showed interesting results that restoration of miR-203 suppresses human SCC metastasis (Benaich et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as information from a recent publication.

claim: miR-203 utilizes the 5′ seed sequences to target perfectly matched sequences located on the 3′UTRs of its target genes.
source: Importantly, with our expansive data set, we confirmed that miR-203 utilizes the 5′ seed sequences to target perfectly matched sequences located on the 3′UTRs of its target genes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the comprehensive target identification analysis.

claim: Trp63 is a well-established miR-203 target.
source: However, we also noted that Trp63, a well-established miR-203 target, showed little change at the mRNA levels under all conditions (not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as background information.

claim: The recognition of the 3′UTR site of Trp63 by miR-203 was robustly detected by the HITS-CLIP.
source: In contrast, the recognition of the 3′UTR site of Trp63 by miR-203 was robustly detected by the HITS-CLIP (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by HITS-CLIP data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: miR-203 antagonizes human papillomaviruses (HPV).
source: We also note that miR-203 is known to antagonize human papillomaviruses (HPV) (Melar-New and Laimins, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as background information from published literature.

claim: Pola1 is a critical cellular gene required for HPV genome replication.
source: Our identification of Pola1, a critical cellular gene required for HPV genome replication, as a target of miR-203 may provide a potential mechanism for miR-203-mediated antagonism against HPV infection.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference based on the identification of Pola1 as a miR-203 target and its known role in HPV replication.

claim: A reduction or increase in the level of miR-203 may be well tolerated by most normal cells.
source: Finally, the relatively mild requirement for miR-203 in slowly proliferating cells suggests that a reduction or increase in the level of miR-203 may be well tolerated by most normal cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the observation that miR-203 has mild effects in slowly proliferating cells.
